newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai currency firms, govt reassures investors.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai currency firms, govt reassures investors.

text.p: Thailand successfully defended its embattled currency on Thursday with a squeeze on liquidity and reassurances that there were no plans to devalue.
The Thai baht, which was hammered by a speculative attack on Wednesday, firmed to 25.350/25.450 late on Thursday compared with Wednesday's finish of around 26.330/26.430.
"The central bank would like to ask the private sector to have confidence in the government policy and not to listen to the rumours," the Bank of Thailand said in a statement.
"The central bank wishes to stress that there would be no devaluation or changes in the currency exchange mechanism which were mentioned by rumours," it said.

In Singapore, dealers said the Thai central bank had ordered local banks not to quote tomorrow/next rates in the baht to offshore parties, effectively cutting off a source of short-term borrowing to fund speculation.

Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on Thursday also repeated the government's determination to guard the currency against speculative attacks. He said in Tokyo the government's defence of the baht has been, and will be, successful.

Rising concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil in the cabinet that could lead to Amnuay's possible resignation triggered heavy baht sales for the dollar on Wednesday. Amnuay has repeatedly denied he would quit.
"(On Wednesday) there was fierce speculation on the baht in the overseas market," the central bank statement said. "At present the situation has eased to a certain degree."

The central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday to defend the baht. Malaysia's central bank and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority also bought the Thai currency, trade sources said, although the intervention was not confirmed.
The Bank of Japan said on Thursday that, if asked, it may intervene in the market to help support the baht under a 1996 Asian currency safety net agreement.

Last year monetary authorities of Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand agreed to establish bilateral repurchase agreements to provide liquidity in times of currency crisis.

Amnuay said that Thailand has support "from all our friends" in its currency defence. He also moved to soothe fears about the deterioration in the Thai economy, saying the country was "in a process of recovery."
The economy had gone through its worst, he said, adding he was pleased with a sharp decline in the current account deficit and inflation, and expectations that exports were improving.
The market rumours also hit the Thai bourse on Thursday, causing the market to drop to near eight-year lows. The main index closed at 557.87 points, a fall of 2.35 percent.
Thailand's currency woes have unnerved other markets in the region with the Philippine peso, the Malaysian ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah also suffering heavy selling.
